issues.legal_issue: A widow’s limited interest in property allotted in satisfaction of a pre-existing right to maintenance becomes an absolute interest when the statutory enlargement of her property rights takes effect.
material_facts: A widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance from her deceased husband’s estate.
Under a compromise decree, she retained a share of her husband’s land in lieu of maintenance, with possession to pass to his adopted son after her death.
The widow later bequeathed the land and died; the adopted son claimed that the decree had left her only a limited interest.
issues.conclusion: The widow’s interest in the land allotted for maintenance became absolute under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the adopted son could not recover it on the basis of the compromise decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) enlarges a Hindu woman’s limited interest in property possessed by her when that property was acquired in recognition or satisfaction of a pre-existing right to maintenance. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi (1977), which held that property allotted under a compromise in lieu or satisfaction of a maintenance right became the woman’s absolute property when the Act came into force.

predicates.widow_property_inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a widow’s interest in property passes to another person after her death.
predicates.female_beneficiary_possessed_property: A woman possessed the property when the law enlarging her property rights took effect.
predicates.property_granted_for_preexisting_mainten: The property was given to the woman in recognition or satisfaction of a maintenance right she already had.

issues.definition: When a widow possessed property granted in satisfaction of her existing maintenance right, her limited interest becomes absolute in a dispute over that property.

issues.legal_issue: The provision enlarging a Hindu woman’s interest in property is not too vague to be construed and applied.
material_facts: The petitioner challenged section 14(1) as vague and relied on observations in an earlier judgment criticizing its drafting.
That earlier judgment had construed and applied the provision to hold that property allotted in lieu of maintenance became a woman’s absolute property.
The Court explained that the earlier criticism urged Parliament to improve the drafting and did not mean the provision could not be applied.
issues.conclusion: Section 14(1) is not vague and is capable of implementation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi (1977), which construed and applied section 14(1) despite comments that its language could cause difficulties and might merit recasting. Those comments did not invalidate the provision or prevent its application.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenged a legal provision’s validity on the ground that its meaning was too uncertain to apply.
predicates.prior_authoritative_construction_applied: An earlier court had construed and applied the challenged provision to decide a case.

issues.definition: A challenged provision is capable of application when its meaning has been authoritatively construed and applied despite criticism of its drafting.

issues.legal_issue: A special provision benefiting Hindu women by enlarging their property interests is not invalid as hostile discrimination against Hindu men on the ground of sex.
material_facts: The petitioner argued that section 14(1) favoured Hindu women on the ground of sex and prejudiced Hindu men.
The provision was enacted to alleviate the restrictions on Hindu women’s interests in property inherited from their husbands.
Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children.
issues.conclusion: Section 14(1) does not violate Articles 14 or 15(1) on the ground of hostile discrimination; it is protected as a special provision for women under Article 15(3).
issues.legal_principle: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on specified grounds, including sex, but Article 15(3) permits the State to make special provisions for women and children. The Court held that section 14(1), enacted to improve Hindu women’s restricted property rights, is such a provision and is protected by Article 15(3).

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenged a legal provision’s validity in court.
predicates.sex_based_objection: The challenger argued that the provision discriminated against people on the ground of sex.
predicates.provision_specially_benefits_women: The provision was designed to confer a special benefit on women.

issues.definition: A provision challenged as sex-based discrimination is constitutionally permissible when it specially benefits women.
